Neonatal mass in the Purplish-backed jay has been documented at approximately 10 grams [Wwb = approximately 10 grams], a value consistent with the altricial development pattern typical of many corvids. Under captive rearing conditions where the ambient temperature was maintained at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the maximum reproductive output per clutch was observed to consist of a single egg [N_R_i = per clutch was observed to consist of a single egg], with females producing between two and three clutches annually [F_R_i = between two and three clutches annually]. This modest clutch size is offset by a relatively high parental investment per offspring, a common life-history strategy among tropical passerines that experience reduced seasonal constraints on food availability. The sexual maturation process, however, does not begin until well after the nestling phase has concluded; gonadal development initiates later in the first year of life, underscoring a protracted juvenile period that allows for the learning of complex foraging and social behaviors before committing to reproduction.

Egg incubation in the Purplish-backed jay proceeds under a distinct thermal regime, as the embryos develop at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a temperature derived from comparative studies of the brood parasite Cuculus canoris and considered representative of typical passerine incubation conditions. Hatching occurs after an incubation period of 17 days [ab = 17 days], yielding altricial nestlings that are entirely dependent on biparental provisioning during the early postnatal interval at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. The timing of this critical life history transition is relatively abbreviated compared to that of some larger tropical corvids, although it aligns well with the incubation durations recorded for other Cyanocorax species. At hatching, the chick's wet weight remains at the neonatal value of 10 grams, and it is during the subsequent nestling phase that the most rapid gains in somatic mass are recorded, as parents deliver insect prey with high regularity throughout the daylight hours.

Under the sustained thermal environment of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] that characterizes the active metabolic conditions of this species, fledging is attained 22 days after hatching [tx = 22 days after hatching]. This developmental milestone marks the point at which the juvenile departs from the nest structure and begins exploratory flight, although it remains in close association with its parents for several additional weeks. The nestling gains mass rapidly during this pre-fledging period, transforming from a near-naked chick into a fully feathered juvenile capable of short-distance locomotion. The 22-day interval to fledging is relatively brief compared to the nestling periods of some boreal jay species, potentially reflecting the reduced predation risk and warmer ambient temperatures of the subtropical dry forests that this species inhabits. Following nest departure, the fledgling enters a critical phase of skill acquisition under the continued supervision of the adults.

Puberty in the Purplish-backed jay is reached at 66 days after hatching [tp = 66 days after hatching], when the gonads become capable of initiating gametogenesis under the thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This relatively early onset of sexual maturation relative to many temperate-zone corvids may be an adaptation to the species' tropical distribution, where longer breeding seasons and reduced overwinter mortality allow for a life-history strategy that favors early reproductive investment. Nevertheless, first reproduction is typically deferred until 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], a delay that almost certainly reflects the social complexity and extended juvenile learning period required for successful territory acquisition and pair bonding within cooperative or loosely colonial breeding systems at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The adult body mass attained by this point reaches the ultimate wet weight of 194 grams [Wwi = 194 grams], a plateau that distinguishes mature individuals from the subadult size classes and that supports the energetic demands of egg production and parental care.

Maximum recorded longevity in the Purplish-backed jay under field conditions in, for instance, the tropical dry forests of western Mexico has been estimated at approximately 5475 days [am = approximately 5475 days], or roughly 15 years, when measured under the typical active metabolic conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This extended lifespan is characteristic of many larger corvids, which exhibit slow life-history strategies involving delayed maturation, low annual fecundity, and high adult survival. The maximum reproductive rate per individual over the course of a year, derived from the clutch size of one egg and the annual clutch frequency of 2 to 3, yields a total of 2-3 eggs per year. This low annual fecundity, combined with the deferred age at first reproduction, suggests that population turnover in this species is slow and that populations may be particularly vulnerable to increases in adult mortality from habitat fragmentation or predation by introduced nest predators.
